root_causes.description: Analytics aggregates are computed on demand by synchronous full scans of the unbounded events table on the single Node event loop, with no covering index on tool_name and no precomputed or cached result.
The Analytics client re-issues the whole bundle on every new_event websocket frame plus a 15 s timer with no in-flight guard or debounce, multiplying the cost of ROOT-001.

findings.problem: The tool-usage aggregate scans every row of events (no index covers tool_name) synchronously on the event loop, alongside several other whole-table aggregates in the same handler, so a large events table stalls the whole server.
findings.performance_principle: Work per request should not grow linearly with total accumulated history, and long CPU/IO-bound work must not run on a thread shared with all other requests.

evidence.statement: toolUsageCounts is SELECT tool_name, COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE tool_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY tool_name ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT 20 with no time or session bound.

No index mentions tool_name: events indexes are session_id, event_type, created_at, (session_id,event_type), (session_id,event_type,json_extract uuid) partial, (agent_id,event_type), (agent_id,created_at), (session_id,created_at). SQLite therefore has no index that avoids reading the table rows for this query.
The handler runs this and the other aggregates with better-sqlite3 .all()/.get(), which block the event loop for the full duration of each statement.

Sibling whole-table aggregates in the same request: eventTypeCounts (GROUP BY event_type, all rows), avgEventsPerSession (COUNT(*) over events), stats total_events (COUNT(*)), dailyEventCounts (365-day range). The scoped variants add session_id IN (SELECT id FROM sessions ...) over events.

A comment in the same file already records that an events-table scan 'becomes tens of seconds and blocks the event loop' on a large DB, showing the authors have seen this failure class for events scans.
No runtime evidence (EXPLAIN, profile, timing) exists in the repository or was supplied.

findings.conditions: Matters when events is large (operators report 'very large'; exact row count unknown) and rows are wide enough or numerous enough for a table scan to take seconds. Negligible on small databases.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for an index or covering index on tool_name, a cache, a materialized counter table, or a LIMIT/time window on this query; found none. The LIMIT 20 applies after aggregation, not before.
Looked for server-side caching or memoization in server/routes/analytics.js; none present. Only dailyEventCounts is bounded (365 days) and can use idx_events_created.

The exact time split between the sibling aggregates is not knowable without a plan or timing; SQLite may satisfy event_type counts from a narrow index, which is cheaper than the tool_name scan of full rows. This keeps confidence at High (mechanism) not Confirmed.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If most deployments have modest events tables, or the SQLite page cache keeps the table hot so scans are fast, the cost is tolerable. Tens-of-seconds reports from operators suggest it is not in the affected deployment, but the per-query split is unmeasured.
findings.recommendation: Stop recomputing whole-history aggregates per request. Preferred: maintain the aggregate incrementally (counter table keyed by tool_name updated at event insert, or a periodically refreshed snapshot) or at minimum memoize the analytics result server-side with a short TTL and a single in-flight computation. Add a partial index on events(tool_name) WHERE tool_name IS NOT NULL as a cheaper interim step so the scan reads a narrow index instead of full rows.

alternatives.option: Partial index on events(tool_name) WHERE tool_name IS NOT NULL (covering for the unscoped query)
alternatives.why: Cheap and quick, reduces I/O per scan but remains O(rows with tool_name) and still blocks the loop; good first step, not the end state.

alternatives.option: Incremental counter table or periodic snapshot for tool and event-type totals
alternatives.why: Removes the per-request O(n) work entirely; read becomes O(distinct tools).

alternatives.option: Server-side TTL cache with single-flight around the whole analytics bundle
alternatives.why: Fast to implement and also fixes PERF-002 server-side, but each miss still blocks the loop for the full scan.

alternatives.option: Move the aggregation to a worker thread or separate read connection
alternatives.why: Frees the event loop but does not reduce total work; useful in addition if scans must stay.

findings.trade_offs: A counter table needs backfill and must stay consistent with event deletes/cascades and the tool_name NULLing migration (server/db.js:540); a TTL cache serves slightly stale charts; a new index adds write cost on every event insert, which is the hot ingest path.

validation.metric: Wall time of GET /api/analytics and event-loop delay of the server while it runs, on a database copy with a large events table
validation.expectation: Direction: the tool_name query switches from SCAN events to a scan of the narrow index (or no scan with a counter table), and event-loop stall during the request drops. Magnitude not derivable from code.
validation.falsifier: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN already shows a covering index scan and the tool-usage statement is a negligible share of request time (profile shows the time is elsewhere, e.g. in pricing).
validation.guard: A server test that asserts EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for toolUsageCounts uses an index, plus an event-loop-delay metric alert on the analytics route.

commands.command: sqlite3 <copy-of-db> "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT tool_name, COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE tool_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY tool_name ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 20;"
commands.purpose: Confirm the scan strategy and temp b-tree for the tool-usage query on a COPY of the database

findings.problem: The Analytics page refetches the full bundle every 15 s and on every new_event, session_created, session_updated and agent_created websocket frame, with no debounce and no in-flight guard, so each open tab can queue back-to-back multi-second synchronous scans.
findings.performance_principle: Expensive idempotent reads should be coalesced and rate-limited so request rate is bounded independently of upstream event rate.

evidence.statement: load() is invoked on mount, every 15000 ms, and in an eventBus subscription for session_created, session_updated, new_event, agent_created and remote refresh messages; no debounce or in-flight check.
The server broadcasts new_event, session_updated and agent_updated for hook ingest events (per event).
Each load calls api.analytics.get() and api.pricing.totalCost(); the server side of analytics has no cache (PERF-001).
The openapi description for the session overview endpoint states the frontend debounces calls on these frames, so a debounce convention exists elsewhere but is not applied here.

findings.conditions: Matters when the Analytics page is open during active Claude Code sessions (frequent hook events) and an analytics call takes longer than the gap between events. Event rate is unknown.

counter_evidence.statement: Looked for a debounce, throttle, abort controller or in-flight flag around load() in the page; none found in the page code reviewed.
Browsers cap concurrent connections per origin and the requests are serialized by the synchronous server, so pile-up is bounded in practice by the tab count and connection cap, but not by cost.
Event arrival rate and whether the websocket is connected during the reported freeze are unknown.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: If the page is opened briefly or on an idle system, only the 15 s timer fires and the amplification is small; the reported freeze may then be entirely PERF-001.
findings.recommendation: Coalesce refreshes: a single in-flight request with a trailing refetch, a debounce of the websocket-triggered reloads, and ideally a server-side TTL cache or ETag so repeated polls within the window cost nothing. Pause polling when the tab is hidden.

alternatives.option: Client-side single-flight plus debounce of event-triggered loads
alternatives.why: Smallest change that bounds request rate regardless of event rate; matches the debounce convention used elsewhere.

alternatives.option: Server-side TTL cache of the analytics response
alternatives.why: Protects against many tabs and clients too, but stale charts and a first-miss cost remain; pair with the preferred option.

alternatives.option: Push incremental updates over the websocket instead of refetching
alternatives.why: Largest redesign for charts that tolerate seconds of staleness.

findings.trade_offs: Charts update at most once per debounce window rather than instantly; a server cache adds invalidation/staleness questions.

validation.metric: Count of GET /api/analytics requests per minute and their overlap while the Analytics page is open during an active session
validation.expectation: Request rate becomes bounded by the debounce/poll window and independent of hook event rate; direction only, no magnitude claimed.
validation.falsifier: Request log or browser network panel shows only the 15 s poll even during bursts of hook events (frames not reaching the page), or requests never overlap.
validation.guard: Client test that fires N new_event frames and asserts at most one analytics request per window.

considered_not_reported.observation: Unscoped path loads every token_usage row joined to sessions and prices it in JS per request.
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Row count is bounded by sessions x models x tiers, not by events; likely far smaller than events, so not the cause of the reported symptom. Cannot be ruled out without row counts.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: token_usage row count is large or the pricing total-cost endpoint profiles slowly
